chem_ocra.15.1.summary: Biological methods of metal extraction provide alternative, low-carbon strategies to recover valuable metals like copper and nickel from low-grade ores, waste rock, or contaminated land. These techniques, specifically phytomining and bioleaching, rely on the natural metabolic processes of plants and bacteria rather than energy-intensive smelting. Although much slower than traditional methods, they are becoming increasingly vital as high-grade ore reserves are depleted and environmental regulations tighten.

core.h: The Global Demand for Metal Extraction
core.p: Traditional metal extraction relies on high-grade ores containing large percentages of metal compounds, but these finite resources are rapidly becoming depleted worldwide.
bullets: High-grade ores are running out, forcing industries to look at alternative sources.
Low-grade ores contain very small amounts of extractable metal, making traditional smelting uneconomical and environmentally damaging.
Biological methods offer sustainable ways to extract metals from waste material and low-grade deposits.

callouts.p: Traditional methods like blast furnaces or direct electrolysis are inefficient and economically unviable for low-grade ores.

core.p: Biological methods use living organisms such as plants or microorganisms to extract metal compounds from ores without the need for high temperatures or massive amounts of electrical energy.
bullets: Two main biological techniques exist: phytomining (using plants) and bioleaching (using bacteria).
Both methods produce a solution containing metal ions, from which the metal can be displaced or electrolysed.
These processes require much less energy than traditional smelting and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

callouts.p: Processes that use living organisms to extract valuable metals from low-grade ores or industrial wastes.
Always refer to low-grade ores when discussing biological methods; they do not work effectively on high-grade ores.

core.p: Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds from soil containing low-grade metal ores or mining waste. The plants concentrate the metals within their stems and leaves as they grow.
bullets: Plants are grown on land containing low concentrations of metal compounds.
The roots absorb metal ions dissolved in the soil water.
Hyperaccumulator plants are specially selected because they accumulate very high concentrations of toxic metal ions without dying.

callouts.p: The use of plants to absorb metal compounds from low-grade ores or contaminated soils.
Plants do not absorb pure metal; they absorb metal ions dissolved in water, which are incorporated into their plant tissue.

core.p: Once the plants have absorbed and accumulated the metal compounds, they are harvested, dried, and burned in a controlled furnace to produce an ash.
bullets: Plants are cut down and collected after a suitable growing period.
The dried plant material is burned inside an incinerator or furnace.
Combustion removes organic matter, leaving behind a concentrated metal-rich ash.

callouts.p: Burning reduces the bulk volume and produces an ash with a much higher percentage of metal compounds than the original soil.

core.p: The metal-rich ash obtained from burning the plants contains metal oxides or compounds that must be processed to yield the pure metal.
bullets: The ash is treated with an acid (such as sulfuric acid) to dissolve the metal compounds.
This chemical reaction creates an aqueous solution containing dissolved metal ions, known as a leachate.
The leachate is separated from insoluble solid impurities by filtration.

callouts.p: Adding acid to the ash creates a liquid solution of metal ions, making subsequent metal extraction much easier.

core.p: Bioleaching uses specific types of bacteria to extract metals from low-grade ores without harvesting plants. These microorganisms break down ores through metabolic reactions.
bullets: Certain bacteria feed on the chemical energy found in sulfide ores or low-grade mineral mixtures.
As the bacteria feed, they catalyse oxidation reactions that release metal ions into solution.
The resulting liquid solution containing dissolved metal ions is called a leachate or leachate solution.

callouts.p: The process of using bacteria to leach metal ions out of low-grade ores, producing a leachate solution.
Bacteria do not require high temperatures, saving significant energy compared to smelting.

fig.cap: Bioleaching mechanism using bacteria on low-grade sulfide ores.

core.p: Whether produced via phytomining ash or bioleaching, the leachate contains dissolved metal ions that must be recovered to obtain the free metal element.
bullets: The leachate is an aqueous solution of metal compounds (such as copper sulfate).
Filtering ensures no solid impurities interfere with the final metal recovery step.
Displacement or electrolysis is then used to extract the pure metal from this solution.

callouts.p: A solution containing dissolved metal ions obtained by treating ore or ash with acid or bacteria.

core.p: Copper can be easily displaced from a leachate solution of copper compounds by adding a more reactive metal, usually cheap and readily available scrap iron.
bullets: Iron is more reactive than copper in the reactivity series.
When scrap iron is added to copper leachate (e.g., copper sulfate solution), the iron displaces the copper.
Equation: Iron + Copper sulfate -> Iron(II) sulfate + Copper.
Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s).

callouts.p: A chemical reaction where a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
Scrap iron is waste material, making displacement a very cost-effective method to recover copper.

core.p: Alternatively, the metal ions in the leachate solution can be extracted by passing an electrical current through the solution in an electrolysis cell.
bullets: In electrolysis, metal ions are reduced at the negative electrode (cathode).
Copper ions gain electrons to form solid copper metal: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu.
Electrolysis produces very pure metal, but requires significant amounts of electrical energy.

callouts.p: Electrolysis gives high purity metal but consumes much more electricity than displacement with scrap iron.

core.p: Biological methods offer profound environmental and resource-management advantages over traditional pyrometallurgical extraction techniques.
bullets: Allows extraction from low-grade ores and mining waste heaps that would otherwise be discarded.
Does not require high-temperature smelting, greatly reducing carbon dioxide emissions.
Conserves dwindling supplies of high-grade copper and other valuable metal ores.

callouts.p: Always mention that biological methods conserve high-grade ores and reduce carbon emissions.

core.p: Despite their environmental benefits, biological methods have significant drawbacks that limit their widespread industrial application.
bullets: Extremely slow processes compared to traditional smelting and blast furnace operations.
Bioleaching can produce toxic sulfuric acid run-off that requires careful environmental management.
Yields of metal per batch are generally low, requiring large land areas for phytomining.

callouts.p: Never state that biological methods are fast; growth of plants and bacterial action take considerable time.

fig.cap: Comparison of advantages and disadvantages of biological metal extraction.

analogy.p: Phytomining is like growing a crop of fruit that selectively absorbs specific nutrients from poor soil, whereas traditional mining is like quarrying massive boulders to smash them apart. Where the analogy breaks down is that fruit is eaten for nutrition, whereas plant ash is burned and treated with acid to isolate pure metal elements.

terms.d: Using plants to absorb metal compounds from low-grade ores or contaminated soils.
Using bacteria to extract metal ions from low-grade ores, producing a leachate.
Rock that contains a very small percentage of extractable metal compound.
A plant adapted to absorb and accumulate exceptionally high concentrations of metal ions.
An aqueous solution containing dissolved metal ions obtained from bioleaching or acid treatment.
A reaction where a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from solution.
Waste iron used as a cheap reducing agent to displace copper from leachate solutions.
The decomposition of an ionic compound using direct electrical current.
Extracting metal from its ore by heating beyond its melting point (traditional method).
The controlled burning of harvested plants to produce a metal-rich ash.
Meeting current resource needs without compromising future generations.
A mixture where a substance is dissolved in water.

mistakes.w: Plants absorb pure copper metal from the soil.
mistakes.r: Plants absorb metal ions dissolved in soil water, which are incorporated into their tissues.

mistakes.w: Bioleaching uses plants to extract metals.
mistakes.r: Bioleaching uses bacteria, whereas phytomining uses plants.
Biological methods are extremely slow compared to traditional smelting.

mistakes.w: Biological methods are used for high-grade ores.
mistakes.r: Biological methods are specifically used for low-grade ores or waste rock.

mistakes.w: Scrap iron is added to molten copper.
mistakes.r: Scrap iron is added to an aqueous leachate solution containing copper ions.

mistakes.w: Phytomining creates greenhouse gases through smelting.
mistakes.r: Phytomining involves burning plants (incineration), not high-temperature smelting.

mistakes.w: Bacteria eat the copper metal directly.
mistakes.r: Bacteria metabolize sulfide minerals in low-grade ores, releasing metal ions into solution.

exam.q: State what is meant by a 'low-grade ore'.
model: An ore that contains a small percentage of metal / metal compounds.
exam.tip: Keep the definition concise and focused on the low percentage of metal.

exam.q: Describe how copper is extracted from low-grade ores using phytomining.
model: Plants are grown on soil containing low-grade copper ore.
Plants absorb copper ions through their roots and accumulate them.
Plants are harvested and burned to produce ash.
The ash is treated with acid to produce a leachate solution.
exam.tip: State the steps in chronological order: grow, harvest, burn, acid treat.

exam.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of phytomining compared to traditional smelting.
model: Advantage: Conserves high-grade ores OR allows extraction from low-grade land / waste.
Explanation: High-grade ores are running out so this uses otherwise useless material.
Disadvantage: Phytomining is very slow.
Explanation: It takes months or years for plants to grow and accumulate metals.
exam.tip: Ensure you give both the point and the explanation for each mark.

exam.q: Explain how bioleaching extracts metal from low-grade ores.
model: Bacteria feed on low-grade ores.
The metabolic processes of bacteria break down the ore.
This releases metal ions into solution, forming a leachate.
exam.tip: Mention bacteria, their action, and the formation of the leachate.

exam.q: Write a word equation for the displacement of copper from copper sulfate using scrap iron.
model: Iron + Copper sulfate -> Iron(II) sulfate + Copper
exam.tip: Ensure reactants are on the left and products on the right with an arrow.

exam.q: State the name of the solution produced by bioleaching or acid treatment of plant ash.
model: Leachate
exam.tip: Learn this key vocabulary term precisely.

exam.q: Suggest why scrap iron is often used to extract copper from a leachate solution rather than electrolysis.
model: Scrap iron is cheap / waste material.
Electrolysis requires a large amount of electricity / is more expensive.
exam.tip: Contrast cost and energy requirements between the two methods.

exam.q: Explain why biological methods of metal extraction do not cause immediate high carbon emissions like blast furnaces.
model: Biological methods do not use high-temperature smelting.
Smelting requires massive energy inputs which often burn fossil fuels.
exam.tip: Focus on the absence of smelting and high temperatures.

exam.q: Complete the half equation for the reduction of copper ions during electrolysis: Cu2+ + 2e- ->
model: Cu
exam.tip: Metal ions gain electrons to form neutral metal atoms.

exam.q: Describe how the pure copper is obtained from the leachate after phytomining.
model: Add scrap iron for a displacement reaction OR use electrolysis.
exam.tip: Two valid methods exist for obtaining the metal from the leachate.

exam.q: State one environmental risk associated with bioleaching.
model: Production of toxic sulfuric acid run-off that can pollute waterways.
exam.tip: Remember that acid run-off is the main environmental hazard of bioleaching.

worked.q: Calculate the percentage mass of copper in a sample of copper-rich ash if 250 g of ash contains 45 g of copper.
steps: Identify the formula for percentage mass: (Mass of element / Total mass of sample) x 100

worked.q: A mining company processes 5000 tonnes of low-grade ore using bioleaching. If the ore yields 0.15% copper by mass, calculate the mass of copper produced in tonnes.
steps: Identify the total mass and percentage: 5000 tonnes, 0.15%
Multiply total mass by the decimal: 5000 x 0.0015 = 7.5 tonnes

chem_ocra.15.5.summary: Recycling materials is essential for sustainable development because it conserves finite natural resources, reduces energy consumption compared to extracting raw materials, and minimises waste sent to landfill. Metals like copper and iron, as well as glass and polymers, can be processed repeatedly to reduce environmental impact. However, life-cycle assessments often reveal complex trade-offs involving collection, transport, and sorting costs.

core.h: 1. The Importance of Recycling and Resource Depletion
core.p: Many raw materials used in manufacturing are finite and non-renewable, meaning they will eventually run out if extracted continuously. Recycling reduces the urgent need to mine new ores or drill for crude oil, helping to preserve the Earth's natural crust and habitats.
bullets: Conservation of limited metal ores such as copper, iron, and aluminium.
Reduction in the volume of waste sent to landfill sites, preventing toxic leaching.
Preservation of landscapes and reduction in habitat destruction caused by open-cast mining.
Decreased reliance on imported raw materials, improving national economic security.

callouts.p: Ores and fossil fuels are finite because they are used up much faster than geological processes can form them.

core.p: Extracting metals from their ores requires huge amounts of energy, often from burning fossil fuels which releases carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide. Recycling often requires significantly less thermal or electrical energy, directly lowering greenhouse gas emissions.
bullets: Recycling aluminium uses up to 95% less energy than extracting it from bauxite ore via electrolysis.
Lower energy requirements mean fewer fossil fuels are burned, reducing carbon footprints and acid rain precursors.
Lower operating temperatures in recycling furnaces produce less thermal pollution.
Reduces sulfur dioxide emissions associated with roasting sulfide ores like copper(I) sulfide.

callouts.p: Always state that recycling 'saves energy and conserves finite resources' when asked for two advantages.

core.p: Metals are exceptionally well-suited to recycling because they can be melted down and recast into new shapes without losing their fundamental metallic properties. Scrap iron can be added directly to a blast furnace alongside iron ore.
bullets: Scrap iron and steel are added to basic oxygen steelmakers or blast furnaces, reducing raw iron ore consumption.
Copper scrap can be melted and cast, or purified using electrolysis to remove impurities if high electrical conductivity is required.
Metals maintain their ductility, malleability, and conductivity after being recycled multiple times.
Magnetic separation is easily used to separate iron and steel from non-magnetic waste streams.

callouts.p: The process of converting waste materials into new materials and objects to prevent waste of potentially useful materials.

core.p: Glass is 100% recyclable and can be recycled indefinitely without any loss in quality or purity. Used glass containers are collected, sorted by colour, washed, crushed, and melted to form new glass items.
bullets: Glass is crushed into a material called 'cullet' before being remelted in a furnace.
Sorting by colour is vital because different coloured glasses contain different metal oxide additives that cannot be easily separated once mixed.
Green, brown, and clear glass must be kept separated in automated sorting facilities using optical scanners.
Melting cullet requires a lower furnace temperature than melting raw materials like sand, limestone, and sodium carbonate, saving fuel.

callouts.p: If glass is not sorted by colour, the resulting recycled glass has an unpredictable tint, limiting its commercial use.

core.p: Plastomers and thermosetting polymers behave differently during recycling. Thermoplastics can be melted and remoulded into new shapes, whereas thermosetting polymers cross-link permanently and char when heated.
bullets: Thermoplastics like poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are shredded, washed, melted, and extruded into pellets for moulding.
Thermosets cannot be melted down because their covalent cross-links prevent chains from sliding past each other.
Plastics must be carefully sorted by polymer type using near-infrared spectroscopy or density separation.
Contamination with mixed polymer types ruins the mechanical properties of the recycled plastic batch.

callouts.p: A polymer that softens when heated and can be reshaped because its chains are held together by weak intermolecular forces only.

core.p: Recycling is evaluated within the context of Life-Cycle Assessments (LCAs), which assess the environmental impact of a product across four stages: extracting raw materials, manufacturing, use, and disposal/recycling.
bullets: LCAs quantify energy use, water consumption, pollutant emission, and waste generation.
Transporting heavy scrap metal to central recycling plants burns diesel and produces carbon emissions, which must be weighed against extraction savings.
Sometimes the energy required to collect, sort, and wash heavily contaminated plastic outweighs the benefits of recycling it.
Designers now aim for 'design for recycling', making products easier to disassemble and sort.

callouts.p: Extraction -> Manufacturing -> Use -> Disposal/Recycling.

core.h: 7. Economic and Practical Challenges of Recycling
core.p: While recycling has clear environmental benefits, several economic and logistical challenges must be overcome to make industrial recycling viable.
bullets: Cost of collection, curbside sorting, and transport infrastructure.
Difficulty and labour intensity of separating complex manufactured goods containing multiple bonded materials (e.g., electronics).
Public participation rates and consumer habits regarding washing and separating waste.
Fluctuating market prices for raw materials; if virgin materials are cheap, recycling becomes economically unviable.

callouts.p: Be ready to explain why consumers might not recycle (time, effort, lack of local facilities) alongside industrial hurdles.

core.h: 8. Detailed Comparison: Raw Extraction vs Recycling
core.p: Comparing the processes side-by-side demonstrates why recycling is heavily promoted by environmental agencies worldwide.
bullets: Mining destroys landscapes; recycling uses existing scrap stockpiles.
Electrolysis of aluminium oxide uses massive electrical currents; melting recycled aluminium uses minimal electrical power.
Sulfuric acid rain risks from sulfide ores are avoided when recycling copper scrap.
Landfill space is preserved, reducing long-term methane gas production from degrading organic impurities.

core.p: In exam questions, you may be given numerical data comparing paper bags versus plastic bags or recycled aluminium versus virgin aluminium. You must use this data to justify a conclusion.
bullets: Look at total energy used in megajoules (MJ).
Examine carbon dioxide equivalent emissions (kg CO2 eq).
Check water usage figures and waste volumes produced.
Always evaluate whether the extraction phase or transportation phase dominates the total impact.

callouts.p: Never state one material is simply 'better' without citing specific data from the table provided in the question.

core.p: Efficient recycling relies heavily on sorting mixed waste streams into pure fractions so that the quality of the recycled product is not compromised.
bullets: Magnetic belts: Used to automatically extract iron and steel objects from mixed municipal waste.
Eddy current separators: Use powerful magnets to repel and separate non-ferrous metals like aluminium from general rubbish.
Optical sorting: Uses infrared lasers and cameras to detect and sort different types of plastics and glass colours at high speeds.
Density floatation: Placing shredded plastics in water tanks where different polymers sink or float based on their density.

callouts.p: A metal or metal alloy (such as aluminium, copper, or brass) that does not contain iron and is not magnetic.

core.p: Recycling is not always carbon-neutral. Policymakers must evaluate the entire operational chain to ensure net environmental benefits.
bullets: Transporting sorted materials long distances by lorry can negate carbon savings.
Chemical washing processes used to clean contaminated plastics generate wastewater that must be treated.
Energy generation mix matters: recycling in a country powered by coal has a higher carbon cost than in one powered by renewables.
Balancing economic viability with environmental protection.

callouts.p: If a 6-mark question asks 'Discuss whether recycling is always beneficial', give points for energy/resource savings and points for transport/sorting costs.

core.p: Modern chemistry is driving innovations in product design and material science to make recycling easier and more efficient.
bullets: Development of biodegradable and bio-based polymers to replace crude oil plastics.
Designing modular electronics that can be easily dismantled to recover precious metals like gold and silver.
Chemical recycling techniques that break down polymers back into their original monomers for repolymerisation.
Standardising polymer labelling to improve consumer sorting accuracy.

callouts.p: Unlike melting thermoplastics, chemical recycling breaks polymer chains down into monomers, creating virgin-quality plastic.

analogy.p: Imagine a town where books are made from rare, handmade paper. Extracting raw materials is like chopping down an ancient forest to make brand new paper from scratch every single time someone wants to read a story—it takes a huge amount of water, energy, and time. Recycling is like returning books to a community library: books are checked, sorted, occasionally repaired, and handed out to new readers repeatedly. This preserves the forest (finite resources) and saves enormous amounts of energy. However, the analogy breaks down because library books last indefinitely with care, whereas materials like plastic degrade slightly in polymer chain length each time they are melted down and mechanically recycled.

terms.d: Processing waste materials into new products to prevent waste of useful materials and reduce environmental impact.
A resource that is being used up much faster than it is formed, meaning it will eventually run out.
An assessment of the environmental impact of a product across its entire life stages from extraction to disposal.
Crushed or broken glass used in glassmaking furnaces to reduce melting temperatures and energy use.
A polymer that softens when heated and can be remoulded because its chains are held by weak intermolecular forces.
A polymer with cross-links between chains that prevent melting; it chars when heated.
A metal containing iron, typically magnetic and susceptible to rusting.
A metal or alloy that does not contain iron and is not magnetic (e.g., aluminium, copper).
A rock containing enough metal compound to make it economically worthwhile to extract the metal.
Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
A device using powerful magnets to repel and separate non-ferrous metals from waste streams.
Breaking polymer waste down into monomers to create new, high-grade polymers.

mistakes.w: Saying recycling creates infinite materials from nothing.
mistakes.r: State that recycling conserves finite resources and reduces extraction needs, but polymer chains can degrade over multiple cycles.

mistakes.w: Stating glass loses quality every time it is recycled.
mistakes.r: Recognise that glass is 100% recyclable and can be recycled indefinitely without any loss of quality.

mistakes.w: Claiming all plastics can be melted down and remoulded.
mistakes.r: Distinguish between thermoplastics (which melt) and thermosetting polymers (which cross-link and char).

mistakes.w: Forgetting that transport has a carbon cost.
mistakes.r: Mention that collecting, sorting, and transporting heavy scrap materials requires energy and produces emissions.

mistakes.w: Saying aluminium recycling takes more energy than extraction.
mistakes.r: Emphasise that recycling aluminium saves up to 95% of the energy compared to extraction from bauxite.

mistakes.w: Confusing ferrous and non-ferrous metal sorting methods.
mistakes.r: Use magnetic belts for ferrous metals and eddy current separators for non-ferrous metals.

mistakes.w: Describing LCA as only measuring carbon dioxide.
mistakes.r: State that LCA measures multiple impacts including water use, energy consumption, and waste disposal.

exam.q: Give two reasons why recycling metals is important for sustainable development.
model: Conserves finite metal ores (1)
Saves energy / reduces fossil fuel consumption (1)
exam.tip: Learn these two standard marking points as they appear frequently in OCR papers.

exam.q: Explain why glass must be sorted by colour before it is recycled.
model: Different coloured glasses contain different metal oxides (1)
Mixed colours produce an unpredictable tint / cannot be easily separated once melted (1)
exam.tip: Be specific about metal oxides and the resulting colour tint.

exam.q: Explain why thermoplastics can be recycled easily, whereas thermosetting polymers cannot.
model: Thermoplastics have weak intermolecular forces between chains (1)
Heating thermoplastics causes these forces to break, allowing them to melt and be remoulded (1)
Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links that prevent chains from sliding, causing them to char when heated (1)
exam.tip: Always refer to intermolecular forces versus covalent cross-links.

exam.q: Describe how iron and steel are separated from other waste materials in a recycling plant.
model: Using powerful magnets / magnetic belts (1)
Iron and steel are magnetic so are attracted to the magnet while other materials fall away (1)
exam.tip: Keep descriptions of physical separation methods concise and scientifically accurate.

exam.q: Evaluate whether recycling aluminium drinks cans is always beneficial to the environment. Discuss both positive and negative aspects.
model: Level 3: A detailed evaluation considering energy savings, resource conservation, transport emissions, and sorting challenges with a clear reasoned conclusion.
Recycling aluminium uses up to 95% less energy than extracting from bauxite ore.
Conserves finite aluminium ore reserves.
Transporting heavy scrap cans to recycling centres burns fossil fuels and produces CO2.
Sorting and processing require infrastructure and energy.
Conclusion: Overall environmental impact is significantly lower for recycled aluminium despite transport costs.
exam.tip: For 6-mark level-of-response questions, ensure you include both advantages and disadvantages before reaching a balanced conclusion.

exam.q: State two stages in a Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) other than extraction and manufacture.
model: Use phase (1)
Disposal / recycling phase (1)
exam.tip: Memorise the four distinct stages of an LCA in correct order.

exam.q: Explain why the energy required to recycle plastic is sometimes greater than the environmental benefit gained.
model: Plastics are often heavily contaminated and require extensive washing with water and chemicals (1)
Transporting low-density plastic waste long distances burns fuel whose emissions outweigh extraction savings (1)
exam.tip: Link contamination and transport logistics to net energy balance.

exam.q: Name the process used to separate non-ferrous metals like copper and aluminium from municipal waste.
model: Eddy current separation (1)
exam.tip: Exact technical terminology is required for top marks.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term 'finite resource'.
model: A resource that is being used up faster than it is formed (1)
exam.tip: Do not just say 'it will run out'; include the rate comparison.

exam.q: Suggest one reason why members of the public might not recycle household plastics.
model: Lack of local council collection facilities / time and effort required to wash and sort items (1)
exam.tip: Practical consumer barriers are standard acceptable answers.

worked.q: A recycling plant processes 5000 kg of copper scrap. If extracting copper from ore produces 4.2 kg of CO2 per kg of copper, and recycling copper produces 0.8 kg of CO2 per kg of copper, calculate the total mass of carbon dioxide saved by recycling this batch.
steps: Step 1: Calculate CO2 produced from extraction: 5000 kg x 4.2 kg CO2/kg = 21,000 kg CO2.
Step 2: Calculate CO2 produced from recycling: 5000 kg x 0.8 kg CO2/kg = 4,000 kg CO2.
Step 3: Subtract recycling emissions from extraction emissions: 21,000 kg - 4,000 kg = 17,000 kg CO2 saved.

worked.q: An aluminium recycling plant uses 1.25 MJ of energy to recycle 1 kg of aluminium. Extracting 1 kg of primary aluminium from bauxite ore requires 25.0 MJ of energy. Calculate the percentage energy saved by recycling compared to primary extraction.
steps: Step 1: Find the energy saved per kg: 25.0 MJ - 1.25 MJ = 23.75 MJ saved.
Step 2: Divide energy saved by primary extraction energy: 23.75 / 25.0 = 0.95.
Step 3: Multiply by 100 to convert to a percentage: 0.95 x 100 = 95%.
